name: Black peel (Chinese peel)

lead: Black peel is an in-clinic chemical peel made from black acetic acid with salicylic acid and other actives. It is used to clear acne and even out skin tone.
In a 2024 split-face study it reduced acne lesions by about 58%, about the same as 25% TCA, with less burning and redness.

paras: The acids exfoliate the upper skin layers in a controlled way so the skin renews. A clinician applies it to light frosting and rinses it off; sessions were two weeks apart in the trial.

Reported effects were mild burning, redness and sometimes dryness or flaking; no pigment problems occurred in the small trial. Peels in general can cause pigment changes or scarring, more so when deeper.

web.title: Black peel vs 25% TCA split-face study (full text)

chain: Chemical exfoliation of the upper skin layers
Fewer acne lesions and more even pigment
angle.text: Black peel is applied in a clinic to exfoliate the skin, and the research describes it reducing acne lesion counts by about 58% over three sessions in one study and lightening hyperpigmentation in a case report. People use it to get clearer, more even skin with less downtime than deeper peels.

lead: Black peel is a dermatology-clinic chemical peel used to improve acne, uneven pigmentation and skin texture. The version described in the medical literature is a superficial-to-medium-depth formulation that combines black acetic acid with salicylic acid, tetrahydrojasmonic acid, biosulfur and potassium iodide.[1] People looking to clear breakouts, fade dark patches such as melasma, or smooth the face use it as a lighter-downtime alternative to deeper peels.[2][3]

Published research is small but real. A 2018 case report described a single session with several passes in a woman with facial hyperpigmentation, framed around peels that boost appearance without prolonged recovery or surgery.[2] A 2024 split-face study of 30 people with mild to moderate acne compared black peel on one side with 25% trichloroacetic acid (TCA) on the other, over three sessions two weeks apart.[1]
infobox: Black acetic acid, salicylic acid, tetrahydrojasmonic acid, biosulfur, potassium iodide[1]
Three sessions two weeks apart in one trial[1]

paras: Black peel has been studied for acne vulgaris and for facial hyperpigmentation including melasma.[1][2] Melasma is a chronic pigment disorder of sun-exposed skin, and the case report places black peel among treatments sought for its cosmetic and psychological impact without the risks of surgery.[2]

The formulation studied contains 50% black acetic acid, 0.5% salicylic acid, 6% tetrahydrojasmonic acid, 10% biosulfur and 0.1% potassium iodide.[1] In the 2024 trial, patients were pre-treated with sunscreen and tretinoin 0.025% for two weeks, a patch test was done behind the ear, and the peel was applied with a cotton-tip applicator to light frosting, then rinsed with water without needing neutralization.[1]

In the 2024 split-face study (30 patients aged 15 to 45), mean total lesion reduction was 57.74% on the black peel side and 57.59% on the 25% TCA side, with no significant difference between sides.[1] Global assessment rated good improvement in 86.7% of black peel sides and 80% of TCA sides.[1]

Burning or stinging was reported in 10% of black peel sides versus 20% of TCA sides, post-peel redness in 6.7% versus 16.7%, and no post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was seen on either side.[1] The authors noted the small sample and the use of a non-standardised grading scale.[1] The 2018 case report described a single session in a woman with facial hyperpigmentation.[2]

Chemical peels in general can cause redness, stinging, peeling, pigment changes and, with deeper peels, scarring, and the risk rises with depth.[3] In the black peel trial no major adverse effects occurred; the reported effects were mild burning, redness, and in a few cases flaking or dryness.[1]
Black peel appears in skin-focused discussion as one of several in-clinic peel options, sometimes called a Chinese peel, alongside TCA and glycolic peels.[3]
